posts.title: Get an alert when a release appears
posts.promise: Watch one public software release page and notify yourself when its version changes.
posts.whatItIs: Simon Willison described asking an assistant to check the actions/python-versions repository hourly until stable Python 3.15 appeared, then tell him. The change was reported, and his post says the version could then be added to a GitHub Actions testing matrix. This is a useful example of a release watcher: a scheduled task repeatedly checks a public source, compares its current state with the previous one, and sends a notice on change. A small student version could monitor one public release page or repository for one chosen signal. The recurring check can run automatically; a person chooses a trustworthy source, confirms that the change means what the alert says, and decides whether to update a project. A possible customer is a small software team that wants timely alerts, but that is a business hypothesis, not evidence of demand.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: small software teams that need timely notices about a few dependencies may pay for a reliable focused watcher; the source establishes no customers or revenue.
loop: Choose one public release page or repository and a specific version signal.
Check it on a schedule and save the observed version with a timestamp.
Compare the new observation with the previous one.
Send a notice only when the chosen signal changes.
Have a person verify the release and decide whether to act on it.
posts.evidence: Simon Willison reports that he asked an assistant to clone the actions/python-versions repository and check it hourly until stable Python 3.15 appeared, then notify him. His post says the release had landed and could be added to a GitHub Actions testing matrix. This establishes one reported working monitoring use, not independent testing, reliability, customers, or revenue.
posts.uncertainty: The source documents one author's example and does not establish alert reliability or demand for a paid service. A student version should monitor one public signal; pages and repository formats can change, and checks can miss or misread releases. A human should verify an alert and choose any software update.
first24Hours: Choose one public repository with a release history and write down the exact version change to detect.
Run a scheduled check that saves the observed version and time, then compare it with the prior result.
Trigger a test notice from a known change and confirm a person can verify the source before acting.

ease.reason: One public repository and one version signal make a plausible beginner project, though scheduling and change detection need setup.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: software teams may value timely release alerts; this source gives no evidence of willingness to pay.

feasibility.reason: A one-source watcher with timestamped comparisons fits a two-week prototype; broad coverage and reliability are unproved.

autonomy.reason: The documented loop checked hourly and notified on a release; people still choose sources and verify alerts.

evidence.reason: The author reports a real hourly check that detected Python 3.15 in the watched repository; it is one attributed example.

steps.message: Reviewed eight ideas from the live snapshot. Picked the release watcher because the source describes a real hourly check and detectable result, and one-source implementation is bounded. Its business demand is unproved; directory-only concepts were rejected for insufficient evidence or underspecified automation. No duplicate among existing posts.
